# Introduction

`repdist` represents proteins in the embedding space of a protein language
model, by default TM-Vec, where cosine similarity between two proteins is
their predicted TM-score. This vignette does two things with that
representation:

- **Group proteins.** `protein_similarity()` and `bin_proteins()` cluster
    structurally similar proteins into bins by Markov clustering (MCL).
- **Find what changed.** `bin_glom()` sums counts within bins, for
    differential abundance testing.

Clustering stands alone: it needs only the proteins' embeddings, and a count
table for the differential abundance step, not `sample_mmd()`. The
[beta-diversity vignette](https://yixuan39.github.io/repdist/vignette.html),
`vignette("repdist")`, covers `sample_mmd()`, installation, and the input
files in full.

```{r libs}
library(repdist)
```

# Data

`simulate_ec` is a simulated metaproteome: 20 samples in two groups over
1,160 bacterial and archaeal Swiss-Prot enzymes with known EC numbers. Each
sample of group A has 5% of its abundance on two extra EC 2.7.7 enzymes,
each sample of group B on two extra EC 2.3.2 enzymes, a different pair in
every sample. `proteins` holds the sequences with precomputed TM-Vec
embeddings, `counts` the samples-by-proteins counts, and `annotation` each
protein's EC labels, used here only to check the bins.

```{r data}
data(simulate_ec, package = "repdist")
proteins <- simulate_ec$proteins
counts <- simulate_ec$counts
annotation <- simulate_ec$annotation
# On your own data: proteins <- embed_proteins("path/on/your/proteins.fasta")
# and counts <- as.matrix(read.delim("path/on/your/counts.tsv",
#     row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE))
```

# Protein similarity

`protein_similarity()` joins two proteins when their alignment has an
E-value of at most 0.01, weighting the edge by their predicted TM-score. It
aligns every pair, so its time grows with the square of the number of
proteins: the 1,160 proteins of `simulate_ec` take about 20 minutes on one
core (`n_cores` parallelises it over several). To keep this vignette fast,
the result below is precomputed and shipped in `inst/extdata`; see
`inst/scripts/make_simulate_ec_similarity.R` for how it was made, with this
call:

```{r similarity, eval = FALSE}
S <- protein_similarity(proteins) # about 20 minutes for 1,160 proteins
```

```{r load-similarity}
S <- as.matrix(readRDS(
    system.file("extdata", "simulate_ec_similarity.rds", package = "repdist")
))
```

# Protein bins

`bin_proteins()` splits the similarity graph by MCL. It returns a list:
`membership`, each protein's bin; `clusters`, the proteins of each bin;
`representatives`, each bin's medoid; and the `inflation` used. The table
below counts bins by size.

```{r bins}
bins <- bin_proteins(S) # Markov clustering
sizes <- lengths(bins$clusters)
table(cut(sizes, c(0, 1, 2, 5, 10, Inf), c("1", "2", "3-5", "6-10", ">10")))
```

`plot_tsne()` draws the embeddings in two dimensions, here coloured by the 12
largest bins. Each bin is a tight group of points; t-SNE keeps neighbourhoods,
not the distances between them.

```{r tsne}
#| fig.width: 7
#| fig.height: 5
#| fig.alt: "t-SNE of the protein embeddings, the 12 largest bins coloured"
set.seed(1)
plot_tsne(proteins, color = bins$membership)
```

The EC labels were not used to build the bins, so they can check them: the
share of multi-member bins whose enzymes all share one EC3 class.

```{r purity}
ec3 <- setNames(annotation$ec3, annotation$protein)
multi <- bins$clusters[sizes > 1]
mean(vapply(multi, function(m) length(unique(ec3[m])) == 1, logical(1)))
```

The [simulation page](https://yixuan39.github.io/repdist/simulation.html)
scores the bins in full: purity, pairwise precision, recall, specificity, F1
and coverage, against MMseqs2 sequence clusters.

# Differential abundance

`bin_glom()` sums the counts within each bin, and the bin table goes to any
differential abundance method; here DEqMS, made for mass spectrometry. It
fits limma's linear model to log2 counts scaled to a common sample depth
and, since a protein measured
by more spectra has a less variable abundance, shrinks each bin's variance
towards a prior that depends on its spectral count. For repeated samples of
a subject, add the subject to the design (`~ subject + group`). Bins seen in
fewer than 10% of samples are not tested.

```{r deqms}
samples <- simulate_ec$samples
bin_counts <- bin_glom(counts, bins) # samples x bins
seen <- colMeans(bin_counts > 0) >= 0.1
depth <- rowSums(bin_counts)
y <- t(log2(bin_counts[, seen] / depth * mean(depth) + 1)) # bins x samples
fit <- limma::eBayes(limma::lmFit(y, model.matrix(~ group, samples)))
fit$count <- apply(bin_counts[, seen], 2, median) + 1 # spectra per sample
fit <- DEqMS::spectraCounteBayes(fit)
res <- DEqMS::outputResult(fit, coef_col = "groupB")
head(res[, c("logFC", "count", "sca.adj.pval")], 3)
sum(res$sca.adj.pval < 0.1) # bins at 10% FDR
```

No bin passes. Each enriched enzyme is abundant in a single sample, and the
enriched enzymes are spread over many bins:

```{r enriched}
enriched <- annotation$protein[!is.na(annotation$enriched_in)]
length(unique(bins$membership[enriched])) # bins holding the 40 enriched
```

A bin of enriched enzymes rises in a few samples of its group, not on average
across all of them, so a per-bin test sees little of the signal; `sample_mmd`
in the beta-diversity vignette tests the whole of it.

# Notes

`protein_similarity()` holds a protein-by-protein matrix and aligns every
pair, so on real data use the proteins identified in your samples, never a
whole search database: 20,000 proteins take about 3 GB and the square of
20,000 alignments; use `n_cores`. Structural similarity does not guarantee
shared function: proteins of unrelated folds can catalyse the same
reaction, and `repdist` measures structure.
